newsitem.title: USA: U.S. June new home sales seen lower, outlook sunny.
newsitem.headline: U.S. June new home sales seen lower, outlook sunny.

text.p: U.S. new homes sales are expected to have taken a slight dip in June, but economists remain optimistic about that sector of the nation's economy.
Experts surveyed by Reuters said new homes sales should decline to an annualized rate of 818,000 from May's 825,000.
The expected drop, said market observers, should be viewed as a correction to very strong sales seen in May.
Annualized sales above 800,000, economists said, was indicative of a healthy housing industry.
June new home sales data will be released Wednesday, July 30 at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
David Berson, chief economist at Federal National Mortgage Association, termed the performance of new home sales "outstanding."
Berson, who expected new home sales to fall off to 810,000, said the dip portends a slight slowdown.
"It is not based on a worsening of fundamentals," he said, noting that the pace of sales has been so vigorous that the expected decline is merely a respite.
"Home sales have been very rapid, so it appears to be unsustainable," said Fannie Mae's chief economist.

Lynn Reaser, chief economist at Barnett Bank Inc, agreed that the cooling off in June's new home sales level should be expected. "It reflects a decline from May which was an exceptional rate," said Reaser, noting, too, that an annualized rate of 818,000 "still represents healthy volume."
Economists agreed that lower interest rates and sunny consumer confidence were behind the heightened activity in the housing market.
Mortgage rates, said Berson, and strong job market have been supportive of home sales.
Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisers in Columbus, Ohio, also pointed out that long-term fundamentals remain favorable.

"Consumer confidence should continue to support the strong level of housing activity this summer," said Barnett's Reaser, noting that while new home sales would remain healthy, they will not see sharp gains. "Pent-up demand has been expended earlier in the cycle," she said.
Berson echoed that sentiment: "I am not sure the numbers can stay this strong forever."

Another factor sure to support new home sales, said Berson, included the presence of a large population of immigrants eager to purchase homes. Those who arrived in the U.S. in the 1980s likely will be looking to purchase homes now, said Berson.
